label: Outcome-Based Pricing Designer
description: Design outcome-based and value-based pricing for professional services. Define measurable outcomes and baselines, structure risk-sharing and gain-share mechanics, set guardrails, and decide when outcome pricing beats time-and-materials or fixed-fee.

claudeKnowledge.description: Professional-services pricing literature (Ron Baker / VeraSage value-pricing, Monitor Deloitte and McKinsey value-based pricing frameworks), gain-share and risk-reward contracting practice (managed-services and BPO outcome contracts, NEC4 target-cost / pain-share-gain-share Option C, IPA / Project 13 alliance contracting), benefit-isolation and engagement-economics references (Phillips ROI Methodology), and ILPA-style fee-and-incentive transparency norms. Use web search to confirm current benchmark fee structures and any client-named contract terms.

guidedInputs.label: Service / Engagement Type
guidedInputs.description: What kind of professional-services engagement are you pricing?

guidedInputs.label: Buyer Context
guidedInputs.description: Where does the buyer sit, and how mature is procurement? This drives how aggressive the risk-sharing can be.

guidedInputs.label: Candidate Outcome Metrics
guidedInputs.description: Which outcomes might the fee attach to? Pick the ones the engagement can plausibly move and measure. Avoid attaching fees to metrics you don't control.

guidedInputs.label: Attribution & Baseline Clarity
guidedInputs.description: Can you cleanly attribute the outcome to your work and establish a defensible baseline? This is the single biggest determinant of whether outcome pricing is viable.

options.label: Clean — direct line of sight, measurable baseline
Shared — client/third parties co-influence the result
Noisy — many external/market factors, weak baseline

guidedInputs.label: Current / Default Pricing Model
guidedInputs.description: What is the fallback you are comparing outcome pricing against?

guidedInputs.label: Deal Specifics, Constraints & Known Concerns
guidedInputs.description: Describe the engagement economics, target outcome size, what you control vs. don't, baseline data availability, the client's risk appetite, margin floor, and any procurement or legal constraints.
guidedInputs.placeholder: e.g. Target run-rate saving ~SEK 40m over 18 months; baseline contested because client reorganised last year; client wants us 'skin in the game' but has a hard cap on success fees; our delivery cost ~SEK 9m; client controls IT change freeze that could delay benefits...

exampleInput: We're a 40-person operations-consulting firm pitching an 18-month procurement-and-supply-chain cost-transformation to a Nordic industrials group. The client's CFO is pushing for 'skin in the game' and dislikes our usual time-and-materials proposal (~SEK 12m). Realistic addressable spend is ~SEK 800m and we believe 5–8% is harvestable, but a chunk depends on the client actually enforcing new supplier contracts, and they reorganised procurement last year so the baseline spend figure is contested. Procurement wants a cap on any success fee and audited savings. Design an outcome-based / gain-share pricing model: how to set the baseline, what share to take, what guardrails and floors we need, how to handle attribution where the client co-delivers, and whether a hybrid (reduced fixed fee + gain-share) beats pure contingency or our current T&M.

exampleValues.known_concerns: Target run-rate saving 5–8% of ~SEK 800m addressable spend over 18 months. Baseline contested after a 2025 procurement reorg. A material portion of savings depends on the client enforcing renegotiated supplier contracts (we advise, they sign). Procurement insists on a cap on success fees and independently audited savings. Our fully-loaded delivery cost is ~SEK 9m; we will not go below a ~25% margin floor on committed time.
